Accents on a Non-Final Atom of a Compound

Maqaf marks join two or more atoms into a single chanted word. In the prose system a chanted word usually has exactly one accent. In a small minority of cases, a chanted word has two accents, but never more than two. Of the 36,786 maqaf compounds in the prose verses of MAM, 233 (0.63%) have an accent on a non-final atom. In every one of them the two accents sit on two atoms of the compound and never both on one, the compound itself having two atoms, or occasionally three. This page counts those cases, sorts them, and asks what they mean for the chanted word

ל֣א־תעש֣ה

in Koren's Deuteronomy appendix Decalogue (the עליון) — a maqaf compound with a munaḥ on both of its atoms. The Wikisource strand Koren otherwise follows in every accent has

ל֣א תעש֣ה

instead: two chanted words, each with a munaḥ of its own.

The odd maqaf in Koren might simply be accidentally carried over from the p-trad תחתון:

לא־תעש֨ה

But if we take the maqaf seriously, is there anything in Tanakh like Koren's two-munaḥ compound?

There is not. No maqaf compound in MAM's prose verses has the same accent on both atoms, not once. Of the 233 prose cases, 211 are a single grammatical category, metigah-zaqef: a qadma before a zaqef qatan.

The prose verses

Two accents can appear on a chanted word, whether it is compound or simple. These are the pairs that occur, in the prose verses of MAM, on a compound with an accent on a non-final atom, and how often each of them occurs on a simple chanted word:

Accent pairOn a compoundOn a simple word
metigah before zaqef qatan211198
mayela before etnaḥta83
mayela before silluq14
merkha before silluq41
merkha before tipeḥa44
merkha before pashta10
mahapakh before pashta33
munaḥ before zaqef qatan1959
Total2331172

Most of these pairs are covered in Yeivin's Introduction to the Tiberian Masorah, §§210, 216, 221, 224, 233 and 241.

Koren's compound

Every one of those cases pairs two different accents: the compound's accent, and a mark of a kind that can precede it. Koren's two are the same accent twice, and no chanted word in MAM is accented that way — so there is no category Koren's compound could be said to be following, and nothing in MAM it could be said to be repeating.

Sharing one of the two accents is no help. The one case whose non-final atom has a munaḥ, Isaiah 40:7

נ֣בל־צ֔יץ

pairs that munaḥ with a zaqef qatan, a pair the table above has.

The nearest thing in a printed edition

None of the printed editions transcribed for these pages has the shape either. The nearest is the Simanim Tiqqun's munaḥ on the joined לא of לא־יהיה and of לא־תעשה — the same phenomenon, a non-final atom keeping its accent, one step short of the same shape, and in this very passage.

The poetic verses

The poetic system is a different matter, and different enough that the same count would not mean the same thing there. It puts two marks on one chanted word readily and systematically (Breuer, Chapter 9 §§20–26), where the prose system does so rarely, and in the few pairs above. And many of its maqafs are not written at all: Breuer (§§27, 37) records that in poetic verses the maqaf after a secondary mark is customarily left unwritten while the atom still counts as joined, so a survey that finds compounds by looking for a written maqaf reaches only part of what is there. MAM's poetic verses have 17 cases by that measure, and MAM has the other part of the measure too: it supplies 116 gray maqafs, its own mark for a maqaf the manuscript leaves unwritten where the chanted word needs one. Of those, 69 join an atom that has an accent alongside the compound's accent; the other 47 have one accent written across the two atoms. Neither figure belongs beside the prose one.
